fullDescription.text: The wallet's message definitions cover Bitcoin, Cardano, EOS, Ethereum and EVM chains, Monero, NEM, Solana, Stellar, Tezos, Tron, XRP Ledger. These chains authorize transactions with ECDSA, Ed25519, Schnorr (BIP-340), which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first. help.text: The wallet's message definitions cover Bitcoin, Cardano, EOS, Ethereum and EVM chains, Monero, NEM, Solana, Stellar, Tezos, Tron, XRP Ledger. These chains authorize transactions with ECDSA, Ed25519, Schnorr (BIP-340), which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first. Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them. Keep the signing layer crypto-agile per chain (algorithm identifiers in messages and storage, room for larger keys and signatures) and track each chain's post-quantum proposals, so that a new scheme can be added when a chain activates it. This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Chains are recognized from the names of the message definitions (.proto files and packages); the schemes are the chains' documented account signatures, not an analysis of the wallet's signing code.

shortDescription.text: Quantum-vulnerable Ed25519: firmware and boot verification (root of trust) (2 file(s))

fullDescription.text: 4 reference(s) to Ed25519 across 2 file(s), e.g. core/embed/sec/image/boot_header.c:81. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: firmware and boot verification (root of trust). These public keys are fixed in the bootloader or the device: with a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) an attacker forges a firmware signature, and replacing the keys needs a bootloader update in the field. Plan a hybrid firmware signature (the classical one plus ML-DSA or SLH-DSA, both required) and the path to ship the new keys in a bootloader update. This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.
